utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted and Alex Demirdjian for the Prosecution, with case manager Thomas Laugel and our intern Simona Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, General. May I remind you that you're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you please take a look at your statement, paragraph 160 -- actually, I think that we can have it on the screen for you too.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph you said, among other things, that you heard from Borisavljevic that Goran Hadzic and Zeljko Raznatovic came to Velepromet on the 19th and 20th of November, 1991. First of all, I'd like to clarify this 19th of November. It says further on in that statement that at the time there were 186 Croat prisoners in Velepromet under the guard of Captain Bajic, that Arkan wanted to take immediate charge of them, but that they were transferred to Ovcara and then taken to Sremska Mitrovica. So now I'd like to ask you, do you know which group of prisoners this referred to because we do know, indeed, that perhaps 186 or 187 prisoners from Ovcara were transferred to Mitrovica and that those were the prisoners who had surrendered at Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, about the date, the 19th. I think that during the previous testimony we did clarify that these dates were unreliable, I mean the people who conveyed this to me. It is the 20th rather than the 19th. That is the first thing that I wish to say. Secondly, I don't know where these people were taken prisoner, the persons referred to here, but I know about that from the 19th, when I was in Vukovar. I was told that they were transferred from Mitnica to Sremska Mitrovica. Possibly selection had been carried out, or rather, a triage. A number of people from Mitnica who were at Velepromet at the time, but I do not know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I wanted to ask you. Further on it says in the same statement that on the next day, the day after this event, at least that's what it says in this statement, the government of the SBWS held a meeting at Velepromet, and at that meeting it was decided to transfer these prisoners to the jurisdiction of the Vukovar TO under the command of Stanko Vujanovic. Is that what Borisavljevic said to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, according to Borisavljevic's words, as for these 186 prisoners that were being asked about, they were transferred to Ovcara and from there to Mitrovica, that is Borisavljevic's version; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if you allow me, I would like to clarify this thing about the session since he moved the date. He did not remember it. I talked to him in 1995. He said a day later and a day after the 19th is the 20th. So since this is not the 19th, but rather the 20th, then probably that day's moved too. That is my assumption. I noted that the date is not certain because there were different versions. People did not mention these -- did not, rather, remember these dates and there may have been a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, he said to you that these were two different days, when he transferred the prisoners from Velepromet to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When Arkan asked for them and when the government meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, we have some information - this is transcript page 5089 - that these prisoners, indeed 187 presumably - prisoners were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica from Ovcara. But we also have information that these prisoners were brought to Ovcara directly after having surrendered at Mitnica. Their names were written down very properly and they were handed over; that is to say, they were not taken to Velepromet at all. Well, all right. If that's what Borisavljevic said to you, that's what he said. But did you hear of this information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which information?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That 187 prisoners or 186 prisoners from Mitnica, that is to say those who surrendered at Mitnica, were transferred to Ovcara directly without being taken to Velepromet or anywhere else, and from there to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have the information that later -- I mean, I know the period --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you just have this information from Borisavljevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about this decision, to hand the prisoners over to the Vukovar TO under the command of Stanko Vujanovic because I see that in paragraph 159 of your statement you mentioned that the commander of the Vukovar TO was Miroljub Vujovic. So I don't know whether Borisavljevic told you about Vujanovic precisely or is this a slip of the tongue, perhaps, with regard to the name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I did not know personally who the commander of the Territorial Defence was in which period. I do have some information from talking to Jovan Vulovic [phoen], a journalist from Vreme because he read things out of his notebook from Vukovar. What he said is one source as to what happened there, and the other source was what Borisavljevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you say that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now I cannot say exactly which one of the two was the commander of the Territorial Defence and which one held a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to look at 1D568, that is number 46 on our list. We have here in evidence a text from the newspapers from that period. The title is: "No Threat of Massacre in Vukovar." This is actually a statement by a representative of the SSNO, Miodrag Starcevic. Do you perhaps remember what position he held at the time, at the SSNO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. He was in the legal sector, in the legal administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You see, if we can just enlarge the B/C/S a bit, the first part, just the first paragraph. He said that the most recent requests of the Croatian government were unfounded because there are no real grounds for fear that anyone in Vukovar will allegedly massacre civilians, the elderly, and children. First of all I want to ask you whether you remember what these most recent requests of the Croatian government were? What was it that they were asking?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know the date. The date does matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. It's the 19th of November. This was published on the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the statement was made a day before that, on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not have any information of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, there's something else that I find striking here in a way. There's a reference to old men and women and children here. Is that a mistake? There is a reference to prisoners of war, imprisoned members of the armed forces. So I wanted to ask you whether you believe that this was omitted by mistake, either by the newspapers or ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, on this 19th of November, I was in the village of Milici, as I said. I could have been in Belgrade too without seeing this text. Since operations were over on the 18th in Vukovar - that's what they say - then the population was taken out of houses, basements, et cetera, and they were evacuated from town. Now, most probably there were some allusions here in terms of their fear, what would happen to these old men. Indeed, elderly people and children, all of those people who had been in the houses until then were getting out. There was this pressure concerning Vukovar all the time; however, it is a fact that the first group that got out expressed their desire to go to Croatia. There was this column - I don't know if I remember correctly - consisting of about 1.000 persons. And then they were returned from the border. The Croats did not want to admit them. Then they were returned to Mitrovica again and then again the Red Cross tried to take care of them. You know what, in that period there was a lot of propaganda going on. There was information then that in some kindergarten some children had been killed. There were all sorts of things that were being bandied about, and I think that this is part of the overall campaign concerning Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 158 you describe, inter alia -- actually, you said one of the officers took care of the bodies, that a bulldozer was used, and so on. I just wanted to clarify something. When you say -- when there's this reference to this burial here, what is meant, the digging of this grave, and then covering it? Or is this a reference to something else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that that was that, the mass grave where the victims were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have another piece of information, that at that time, on the 19th of November, to be precise, among other people General Jerko Crmaric was in Vukovar too. And our information says that at that time he was assistant commander for logistics in the 1st Military District, I think. Have you heard about this? I assume that you did not see him because you said that you did not see anybody else except for the security organs that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know General Crmaric and it is correct that he held the position of assistant commander for logistics in the 1st Military District, but I am not aware of his being in Vukovar. I did not see him and I did not receive any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have here in evidence a document, 1D584, again on our list this is number 51. It is a document -- it is actually a set of instructions regarding persons who are held by the JNA during internal conflicts, and I see that he is precisely the person who gave these instructions and it says there what is done with such persons. Tell us, was General Crmaric in the security organs before he held this position?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he came to that position after being a security organ, but he was in that service for a while during some previous years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this instruction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was preparing to testify in the proceedings in Croatia, I had an opportunity to see it. And I can say that this instruction followed from another instruction that was drafted at SSNO level following the orders of the Chief of General Staff, Blagoje Adzic. And then it was sent down to the commands of army districts and then they elaborated some details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I tender this document and previous document. I forgot to ask it immediately. It is 1D568 and 1D584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits D100 and D101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you one more thing. You saw in documents and probably also learned later that the 20th of November was the most critical day, and this is basically why we are here involved in these proceedings, at least as far as Vukovar is concerned. And according to our information, at that time during those critical 72 hours, starting from the evening of the 19th of November until the late evening hours of the 20th of November, there were a total of ten officers from the security organs in Vukovar. You said that they were from the 1st Army District, whereas our information was somewhat different. We were told that some were from the security administration, others from the 1st Army District, but you said something else. There was also Marko Crmaric. Did you ever hear why it was necessary to have such a large number of people with much experience in this line of work during those 24 or 36 hours?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I still stand by what I said in relation to the security organs. There weren't ten of them. I think that there were five, including the warrant officer who was there. Now since you're alleging that there were ten security organs there, which I denied and I asked you for their names - but please don't interrupt me now - and you're asking about General Crmaric, whether he was in security, that has nothing to do with the matter. He was the assistant commander for logistics in the 1st Army District. This instruction about treating persons who -- and so on was drafted by the assistant for logistics of the federal secretary of national defence, General Sivic. And this instruction at the level of the 1st Army District was drafted by the assistant for logistics, General Crmaric, and at the time he was not in the security organs. And you are saying: There were ten of them and how come there was such a large number? There were people from the 1st Army District because we are talking about a complex activity which consisted in the evacuation of persons from the town, and then of course senior officers had to be sent there. And he did have some experience and had some duties under this instruction. There was even a commission, I think, which was appointed in the 1st Army District did which did not include security organs. If the commission with Crmaric was there, then I can understand that, but they are not part of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You clarified this sufficiently. Among other things, General, in the examination-in-chief on page 7952 and the following of the transcript, you explained why the JNA could not occupy Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem because these areas were part of Yugoslavia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit -- an exhibit from the 65 ter list, number 644 was shown to you. That's a statement - you may remember - made after the liberation of Vukovar when Goran Hadzic spoke and said that the worst ones were to be tried at Vukovar and we already have it on our screens. And among other things, he said that they were to be tried in Vukovar and in the second or third instance possibly in Serbia -- or actually Yugoslav courts were to decide about that. And you stated your opinion that it wasn't possible because they were not a constituent part of Yugoslavia. If I remember well, that was your explanation. Here's what I want to ask you: Do you know that even before the war in that territory there was a court in Vukovar and one in Beli Manastir and so on, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do tell me now, if the state that existed then and the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as well as the JNA considered this territory part of Yugoslavia, why do you think that there was an obstacle for the courts in Belgrade or -- and Yugoslavia to reconsider the decisions of courts in Vukovar or Beli Manastir? Of course this is a legal matter and you're not a lawyer, but perhaps you can explain nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will speak about the practical aspect. You say that there were courts in Vukovar, Beli Manastir, Osijek, and so on, but there was also a Territorial Defence with its staffs in Vukovar, Beli Manastir, and so on, but it was no longer the case. And so that was a new situation. I don't know whether the courts you are talking about were operational at the time at all; for example, the court in Vukovar. I would like to know what kind of cases they tried, given the crimes that had been committed. I don't know if the courts were even in existence at the time. And even if they were, whether they were operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but were you obliged to know these things as the security organ, or rather, the chief of the security administration of the SSNO, whether the Vukovar court was trying cases and passing judgements?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course I'm not a jack-of-all-trades. But in principle, as for the demand that the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to be recognised as part of the armed forces of the SFRY, the decision was negative, they were not recognised as such. And that decision was sent not only to the -- or rather, that demand was sent not only to the SSNO but also to the Presidency. And as far as I know, it was ignored.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we can clarify one more thing. You're speaking about the decision about the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to become part of the armed forces of the SFRY. That's the decision you're talking about. Under the criterion that were applied then, the members of the TO were under Yugoslavia, but that Territorial Defence was undermanned and there was a lot of desertion and evasion of conscription. Why was there opposition to make this TO part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia? Even in such a situation when there are people -- when there were people who were willing to take part in combat, and according to what you know such a decision was not taken?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were -- they had been members of the TO of Croatia previously, and now there were autonomous provinces that had been established and they were not legally defined as territorial units that were part of Yugoslavia. There had to be a staff at some level that had to be equal to the provincial staffs of Territorial Defence. Such a staff existed in Kosovo. You as a lawyer certainly understand that situation much better because there was this province that seceded from Croatia, it proclaimed its existence, but organisationally speaking it wasn't officially part of Yugoslavia, the SFRY. And what we were discussing here, that in the first phase they were arming themselves individual to protect themselves, and later they were provided weapons in a more organised fashion. And they had some internal material organisation of their own in place, such as staffs and so on. That was not an obstacle. Whoever was willing to defend Yugoslavia together with the armed forces and the TO from Vojvodina and the JNA, to do so, to take part. And that's why there were those instructions about the acceptance of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We saw documents about some TO detachments from Borovo Selo, Trpinja, or whatever were involved in some combat activity under the command of JNA units, but I don't want to dwell on this because this is another matter after all. Instead, I'll return to the text on the screen. Have you noticed that this deals with trials, that we see the headline: "The Worst Will be Tried in Vukovar," the most hardened as we see here. It's not only about taking people to court and trying them, but those who have committed serious crimes and there is enough evidence to prove that, that they should be tried there. I think that you were -- that you said that they were saying that they wanted try all prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they wanted to try all prisoners but that they wanted to take over all of them, because they had their judiciary system that will launch and follow up proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find that in this text?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is what I stated here. Another matter is interesting now and to my mind it is still interesting today. Were there judicial proceedings that were conducted against those 100 or 200 at Vukovar -- at Ovcara and were they sentenced to death? Was anything like that done? And how were they judged?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as of the 20th when they took them over, was it a court-martial or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But whoever mentioned a court-martial? Where did you find that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no I'm interested if that was the case. They are saying they had their own judiciary. When they took over those prisoners, they probably had to be tried somehow and be sentenced to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But when do you think that they should have been tried and convicted, during what time? A week? A month? Three months?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not a valid reply to my question. I'm commenting on this from the aspect of this statement, sir. Mr. Hadzic said we have our own judiciary and we will try them. But did they? Were these people tried? They got these prisoners, they were in charge of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAO government at its session at the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Panic was sent by the brigade command to that session --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, gentlemen, gentlemen, you are overlapping all the time. Even if you need to interrupt the other party, if I may say so, you interrupt and then wait for the interpreters to finish the interpretation and then you say what you have to say. So please be careful, pauses between questions and answers, and no interruption, no overlapping, and interruption only with also a pause. Thank you. Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's my understanding that we did not get his full response to the last question. He was interrupted --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- we just have "General Panic." If he could repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do agree. Let's repeat the last question and the last answer, and slowly, please. Have a little bit of compassion with the interpreters, who have a very hard job with you -- with both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question was when you learned that the government had taken over the prisoners. And your answer was: The government took over the prisoners -- just a minute. I apologise. That the government was in charge of the prisoners, the SAO government, at its session of the 20th of November. And I asked from whom you heard that and you said some names now I think that it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I asked you whether there were -- there was a proceeding instigated against them, whether they were prosecuted, and what the outcome was, and I didn't get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just tell you -- say one thing to you: Do you know when the Ovcara grave-site was discovered? If you don't know, I'm not insisting on this question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to our information, this only happened in late 1993 and there was a lot of work that needed to be done, the exhumation, the establishment of the identities, and so on, and I'm sure that you know that it's impossible to prosecute anyone or to instigate proceedings without that information. However, I'd like to say something else, General. You were a witness in this case that was prosecuted in Belgrade, the Ovcara case. Do you recall how long the trial went on for? And this is in peace time, not war time.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a witness in two cases and the case before a military court in Belgrade against unidentified perpetrators of crimes, and I believe this trial was relatively short, perhaps a month or two long, but this is just my conjecture. I -- and then it was concluded that the military -- the military personnel were not responsible for that, but the perpetrators were never uncovered. That is the first trial that I was a witness at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what year this was in? Was this in 1999, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I think in early 1999, before I was re-activated, and I appeared as a witness before a war crimes court in a case which took a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1999 the military court did not identify the perpetrators, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were in -- they were responsible -- they tried military personnel, first of all, if such were perpetrators, but according to the procedure, as far as I know, because the perpetrators were never identified then they transferred the case to civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe the reason was that the military courts were abolished, but let's not dwell too much on that. I believe you appeared as a witness again in 2005 in the case where there were some 15 accused or so and they were all convicted later on. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this trial went on from, what, 1999 to, what, 2007 or so? Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. The proceedings began, the trial began, in 2005 and it went on until 2007. But there were two different proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you're not taking into account the investigative phase of the proceedings that -- the investigation that was conducted by the court?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are now going into legal issues and I'm not really an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the text we have before us. Could we take a look at the last portion of this text. It says that at this government session Arkan -- Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan, was present. This is in the second column on the right in the B/C/S version. And I believe in the English version, that's at the -- it starts at the bottom of the page and then goes on to the next page. It says there that his unit -- that one of -- he says: "'My unit is one of the proofs that the force, the strength of Serbia, is endless and all of us who fought at Vukovar, we were under the unique command of the JNA which had wonderful officers of all ethnicities...,'" and so on and so forth. So he publicly states here that he was under the unified command of the JNA. Do you know whether anyone ever -- any officers, JNA officers, ever refuted this? Was this correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was ever denied by anyone. I believe that for the most part his words or he was ignored and they didn't feel that it was necessary to comment on it at all. But I would also like to go back to a portion of the text, if you allow me, but maybe it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can quote any part of the text, the entire text that you see before you. If you find that there is something more relevant, please tell us so.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on this date and in relation to the document that you showed of the -- of 10th December 1991, the document from the Novi Sad Corps, the manpower, and the Arkan's men, that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that document is dated somewhat later. It's a December document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I said, a document of 10 December. So what would he be doing there at this session of government as a member of the Novi Sad Corps together with Goran Hadzic? I mean, if anyone from the JNA should have been there, it would have been Biorcevic, not him. So I'm just trying to point out who he was and what he was. He never wore the JNA uniform and that he should comment on the JNA and say that he was a member of the JNA, whereas he slapped those JNA soldiers on two occasions and -- that's one of the reasons why the proceedings were instigated against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, very well you just reminded me of something. When speaking about the government session, and I'm referring to the time when I -- where we overlapped and the interpreters were unable to interpret the whole thing, you mentioned two names, in fact, two names of people from whom you heard what had happened at the government session. And I'll remind you. You mentioned Bogdan Vujic and Lieutenant-Colonel Panic who at the time was the deputy to the then-Colonel Mrksic. Can you confirm that you mentioned these two names?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: Did you trust Bogdan Vujic or did you believe him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you asked what about, was there something that you wouldn't believe him about or wouldn't trust him with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believed him in relation to the time when he was in active service and when I had official business with him and when I took part in some missions together with him. Now, as to whether I would believe or trust him after that when I had no contact with him, all I could do was assess what was correct and true of what he was saying, if I could compare that to information from other sources. Let me be more specific. He claimed that he had been sent both to the collection centres, including Ovcara I suppose, by the security administration, and that is how he introduced himself when he came to Velepromet, that he came from the security administration. But he was not from the security administration, he was a retired officer, and we did not have any officers in the security administration who had any war duty. And he was sent there by the chief of security of the 1st Corps, and I -- that's the 1st Military District, and in that sense I cannot believe that portion of his statement. But as for the rest, I did trust him at the time when we had -- we were assigned -- we participated in joint assignments and when I really had no objections to his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, according to some information he represented himself as being from the security administration and you believed this not to be true because he was not really recruited by the security administration. And I'm talking about the period when he had already retired, the period of war from 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to Sremska Mitrovica now. According to your information, the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem government and Goran Hadzic went to Sremska Mitrovica on two occasions, including Goran Hadzic [as interpreted], asking to be involved in the investigation, to be shown the list of prisoners. And on both those occasions, they were denied access. The first time this was denied by Maksimovic, and the second time you were the one who told them that this could not be done. Were these the only two contacts that you know about where they came to Sremska Mitrovica with such requests? I'm talking about the period after Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was also mention of weapons and under threat of weapons, that they would take over these prisoners and so on. Could you tell me, on those occasions when they came there, were they armed? When they talked to you, for instance, were they armed or did they come there unarmed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have long barrels. Whether they had some personal weapons, I don't know, sidearms, I don't know. That was something that was to be taken care of by the duty officers who allowed them to come in. But as far as I know, the standing order was that no one could come in armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, that was not visible? In other words, you couldn't see that any of them had any weapons, at least on those occasions when you were in contact with them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more thing. Did you find it at all strange that they should come there, to the prison, and demand to be handed over prisoners from the person who was in charge of those prisoners and that they never addressed them -- their request to superior authorities, higher authorities, maybe the JNA or the Government of the Republic of Serbia or some authorities in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did submit requests earlier; specifically, on the 27th of November Mr. Susa as the minister of justice sent a letter to the commander of the 1st Military District, Colonel Panic, with the same request that I mentioned earlier were addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, there was no positive response to that in any sense nor did they invoke this when they talked about you. They never mentioned that there was a positive response to a request of theirs, that they should take over these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, this is a bit confusing to me. Now, if they could come to the prison warden, Maksimovic, that they should go there and ask to take over the prisoners, although their requests had not been approved earlier. That would be strange. In other words, addressing a lower-level official in the chain of command when superior officers or higher officers, they did not get anywhere with that request, with the higher officers?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Maksimovic was not the prison warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for using that term. That's correct, he wasn't the prison warden, but he was a lower-level officer with lower-level duties vis-a-vis the prisoners and vis-a-vis the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you but I don't understand what the question was, why they would address lower-level organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know the answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, other than that they had tried at a higher level and they didn't get anywhere. Now they were trying to do it at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to clarify a few more things from your statement. At paragraph 102, for instance. You were shown an exhibit in this paragraph -- I apologise. It seems I got the wrong number -- the wrong paragraph number. No, that's the wrong paragraph. My apologies. Paragraph 99, please. In this paragraph you said, among other things, that Hadzic resisted taking on active-duty JNA officers as commanders of the SBWS TO. According to the information that I have, he was never asked anything like that, whether he would accept or not someone as the commander, especially not where military officers were concerned. So I wanted to ask you: Where did you get the information from?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't up to the JNA to appoint those officers. They can send or appoint officers at a request, pursuant to a request; however, these officers, there was never a request from Goran Hadzic for these officers. That's one thing. And secondly, he was always negative about JNA members and personnel. If I can remind you of his words of gratitude after the Vukovar operation and who the persons that he thanked for the operation were, he never mentioned the JNA. He thanked the Serbia organs, I suppose he meant the Serbia MUP, but not the JNA. He never thanked the JNA. He frequently spoke about treason within the JNA, his distrust of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to go into that, first of all, because I don't have enough time. And as for criticism of the JNA, that did happen and you know that it came not only from Goran Hadzic but many others too, but I really wouldn't want to discuss all of that now. So, in other words, you are saying that he never asked that active-duty officers of the JNA be appointed commanders in the TO of these units of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; that's your answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he was the one in charge to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, being president of a district, he can appoint military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to ask you. Do you make a distinction between a president and a prime minister? You do understand that difference, do you? You know that, say, the prime minister of Serbia or Yugoslavia had no jurisdiction over the Territorial Defence. Say the president of the Republic of Serbia specifically, you even spoke about that, he had jurisdiction over the TO of Serbia but it was the president who did, not the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says there organs of the social political community propose persons for command positions in the Territorial Defence, and the Presidency of the SFRY verifies that. So it doesn't say whether it's the prime minister. Again, we are going into legal squabbles. He admitted Arkan, he probably didn't ask for him either, but he tried to impose himself through Badza and we discussed this many times --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you're doing it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing, this is paragraph 107 of your statement. You said -- you spoke about a meeting, actually. You spoke about a meeting that was held on the 25th of February, 1992, that was attended by Panic, Mandaric, Stanisic, Stojicic, and you also mentioned Goran Hadzic. According to my information, Goran Hadzic did not attend such a meeting. So can you tell us where you got this information that he personally attended that meeting? I mean, I'm not saying whether the meeting was held or anything like that. It's his presence that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs at the forward command post of the 1st Military District, I heard it from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give the name of this person now or should we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Petkovic then, Colonel Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He is no longer alive to the best of my knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I just wanted us to take a look at these questions related to town commands. You said that that was not your line of work but you did provide certain answers in relation to town commands. You also said that they had some kind of a consultative role, advisory role. In a way they only assisted the civilian authorities in carrying out their duties. Could we please take a look at that instruction that exhibit shown to you, that is, Exhibit 708.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 65 ter, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an instruction. This is actually a letter through which this was communicated; however, it does say that separate tasks would be sent in as well and that was sent on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see here in paragraph 1, tasks from the area of state administration, legislative, judicial, and executive authority. And it says there what it is that organs -- security organs do -- sorry, it wasn't security organs. It is actually town commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at what paragraph 9 says. "Direct co-operation with organs of the judiciary and proposing measures with a view to the efficient functioning of the judiciary, judicial administration, and other judicial institutions." Do you think that this was a reason why the then-minister of justice of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem sent some requests, or rather, why a delegation of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem wanted to participate in these investigations that were carried out and to play a more active role in all of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that calls for speculation as to what the minister of justice was thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think that these were legal grounds on the basis of which the organs of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem could have asked for participation in investigations that were underway in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When he asked for that, these instructions hadn't even reached him, hadn't even arrived in the area, because it was on the 27th of November that he addressed the 1st Military District, not the judicial organs, military judicial organs in terms of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that this is co-operation that is supposed to take place between the civilian organs and the town commands with the judicial organs from the territory -- well, all right. After all, I just wanted to ask you, you've given your answer. Can we now move on to the second chapter. Things are a bit more specific there. Paragraph 6, please. You see, until then there were references to direct co-operation and participation in that and so on. However, in paragraph 6 it says what the task is in the field of security of the organs of -- for civilian affairs: "Undertaking carrying out certain investigative actions and pressing criminal charges against the perpetrators of criminal acts." I have the impression from this particular wording that town commands or organs for civilian affairs were supposed to do that without co-operation or consultations with local organs of government. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in paragraph 5 it says: "Co-ordination of activities and establishing direct co-operation with the organs of government in preventing and uncovering criminal acts and discovering and capturing perpetrators and take it before the authorised judicial organs." So they're not the only ones for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're talking about 6.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm talking about -- sorry that I interrupted you. I'm talking about paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, paragraph 5 speaks about certain activities and paragraph 6 speaks of other activities. I'm asking you about paragraph 6, if your understanding is that it's one and the same thing, I have nothing against that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can explain that they cannot take these measures regarding crimes that they are not in charge of and military organs are in charge of crimes referred to in chapter 25, and that has to do with military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That is your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it is according to the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This has to do with a specific territory where there is still a military administration. At any rate, I'm not going to insist on your answer to that question. Let us look at paragraph 11 now. Again, this is a task that is supposed to be carried out by the town command -- rather, the organ for civilian affairs. It says: "Administrative duties with regard to procurement, holding and carrying weapons and ammunition and issuing approvals in that regard." And that also shows that it was only the town commands that were in charge of that; that is to say, organ for civilian affairs. Can you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree. This entire instruction does not refer to the tasks of these organs, the ones that they carry anyway; rather, they are instructing civilian organs how to take over this work and then they're saying what the activities are that they should co-ordinate together and to help them become more independent. Sorry, the Presiding Judge is going to blame me again if I cannot say all of this in a flowing manner. It's not that they are the mainstays of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you think, why doesn't it say: Advising civilian authorities in carrying out administrative work and so on? Why would that have been omitted precisely in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because in the general remarks in this document it says what the tasks are, that is, first and foremost making the civilian organs capable of taking over these functions and doing their own work. It always says "render assistance to" and so on. It's not for them to carry out the tasks that are referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now move on to chapter 5 and that is on page 6. Two pages ahead, please, page 6. Yes, that would be it. We're just waiting for the English text to appear as well. Sanctions are established here. "Sanctions to be taken in case of failure to comply with order, instruction, and suggestion ... by the organ for civilian affairs. With regard to the establishment and the functioning of the authority, system, economic and social activities." And you see that sanctions are listed there, the ones that are practically under the jurisdiction of the courts. That is to say that the law states what kind of measures can be taken; that is to say, imprisonment, fines, et cetera. So this shows that these sanctions are prescribed herein and it says that it is the civilian -- the organs for civilian affairs, or rather, town commands that are in charge of this. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree if you read the rest of this sentence; however, these provisions are applied if they are not in contravention of the provisions of the Criminal Code of the SFRY. And that would be the case if military organs were to take measures against persons who had not committed crimes or had been suspected of committing crimes that fall under the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us look at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let us look at what, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry? Paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to the previous page. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could we please move on to the next page. I do apologise. I think that I did not mark these paragraphs properly. Yes, this is at paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We should read it in its entirety. "Besides the above, in the work of the organs of civilian affairs, certain situations will dictate the use of procedures and measures as per the regulations of the combat use of the JNA units and the procedures which regulate the use of military police." Now the following sentence is very important. "The order of the commanding officers should ... the execution of the said not constitute a criminal act, is legally binding." Do you agree that the commander, or rather, that the senior officers of town commands or the ones in civilian affairs could issue orders that were legally binding, of course if the execution of that order is not a criminal act?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that pertains only to certain situation which will dictate such measures. So this is an exception, rather than acting in accordance with rules and regulations. I suppose that this is about an extraordinary situation when, say, on the ground a terrorist group appears. And then you act in line with the rules and regulations about the combat use of units and you engage a military police unit. Because in normal situations, it would be the organs of the MUP who are in charge of such matters rather than the army, but only if they can't cope then the military police takes action. So this would only apply in extraordinary situations, in exceptional situations. This is not a rule. This is an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us agree first. This does not say in extraordinary or exceptional situations. It says "certain situations," that is, some situations. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you a couple of questions more because time is running out. Among other things, you spoke about the Krajina. A Prosecution exhibit was shown to you, number 1058, which is from the OTP list under number 133.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, could you finish your cross-examination before the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say this is a report, to call it that, which, let's take a look at the last page, which Milan Martic who at the time, I believe, was minister of the interior or minister of defence - I don't remember all that precisely - in which he reports about some talks that Goran Hadzic and some other members of the then-government of the RSK had with some internationals. The content itself is not essential. I'm interested in the first page, if we could see it. Here we see who this was sent to, or rather, who he was writing to, and we see it says to B. Jovic personally, I take this to be Borisav Jovic. And then J. Stanisic and then A. Vasiljevic, the security administration of the SSNO. Now, tell me, please, did you receive such reports from the organs of the RSK in 1992, practically until you withdrew from your position on the 8th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received reports along professional security organ lines. These persons are mentioned here, including me, probably because we had had a meeting at Plitvice where there were talks with the Krajina organs about the demilitarisation of that zone and the establishment of TO units. I don't remember getting this, but if I did get it I don't see a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you one more document. It's from the OTP 65 ter list -- actually, it's an exhibit, P2915. It's number 214 on the OTP list. This is a report of the committee for monitoring cease-fire. It says that two ministers of -- two government ministers of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem attended a meeting with Croatian representatives and people from the JNA. Now, tell me do you know, based on this report or independently of it, that government ministers attended this meeting? I'm asking because according to our information the people who attended that meeting were not government ministers. I'm referring to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of such a meeting and, much less, who attended it. This was at local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- maybe I would have five minutes after the break, maybe, if you could -- with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zivanovic, you will have five minutes before the break. Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to consult my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you'll have five minutes after the break. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: General, we will take our break now. We come back at 11.00. As usual, the court usher will help you to go out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To inform the parties, the afternoon session is organised, so that's okay. We will sit from 3.00 to 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, please take a look at paragraph 155 of your statement. You speak here about some dead bodies that were found by military police patrol and that further investigation into the case was left to the SBWS MUP. The military police took video footage and took down the necessary details, and please tell me what this means precisely, "informed the MUP ." Did they just tell them: We found this or that? Or did they also give them the footage and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not acquainted with these details. Under the law it was sufficient to secure the site and to inform the MUP over the radio or by phone, and then they would be obliged to go to the site. But what they in fact did, I don't know in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who informed you of this in the first place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it may have been the security organ of the 1st Military District. It was long ago, so I don't remember that detail. But it would be natural to assume that they first informed the security organ of the 1st Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That would mean Milic Jovanovic, who was a head of the security organ of the 1st Military District at the time -- oh, I apologise. I made a mistake. It would have been General Babic then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One more question, General, my last. During this cross-examination that went on for three days, I showed you a number of documents and you offered us your conclusions, your opinions, your interpretation. And I asked you at the beginning, if you remember, whether you had a biased attitude toward the JNA. Let me now ask you if in your answers during this cross-examination when you were interpreting documents you were biased with respect to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered in the affirmative to your question if I am proud to have been a JNA officer. I have nothing to add to that. I suppose that you're also proud of your profession. That does not mean, though, that due to the fact that I am proud to have been a member of such an army I'm biased in giving evidence. I have tried to speak the truth as far as my memory allows me. Not going into the question who was to blame. In my statement there's something that you did not use. When I said that Mrksic was responsible to introduce law and order in Vukovar in line with his powers rather than his Chief of Staff being attacked there and him failing to do anything about it. I really tried to speak the truth because I'm testifying in court and I'm willing to be held accountable for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't doubt that, but I asked you really a simple yes/no question. Do you think that since you were a member of the JNA for a long time may have influenced some of your conclusions while you were interpreting some documents? That's all. I don't doubt that you spoke the truth about facts.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My having been a JNA member did not influence my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I have no more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Olmsted, re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to, as briefly as possible, clarify some of the matters that were raised during your cross-examination over the last couple days. Firstly, yesterday Defence counsel showed you an SSNO order to Zeljko Raznatovic, sending him to Bijeljina, which you testified was a forgery. This is at transcript page 8104. And you also testified yesterday that Arkan was in Bijeljina sometime around March 1992. While in Bijeljina, how did Arkan and his units behave towards the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would object because Bijeljina is in Bosnia and Herzegovina and it is not a part of this indictment; it is irrelevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, it -- I think, Your Honours, if you give me a little leeway you'll see where I'm going with this issue -- or at least where I anticipate seeing where it goes. But the topic of Bijeljina did come up. It's even mentioned in this -- that's what this order is with regard, and so I just want to ask some contextual questions before I get to the point I'm trying to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This order was not admitted into evidence and also is irrelevant for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me get to the point, Your Honours. My point is with regard to Arkan in particular and his behaviour and his chain of command, which is relevant to this case, regardless where he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, could you answer the question with regard to Arkan and his unit's behaviour in Bijeljina towards the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. On the 1st of April, 1992, there was unrest in Bijeljina. Serbs and Muslims clashed, if I can put it that way. And then Arkan's unit barged in from Badovinci. They acted very cruelly. As far as I can remember, there were about 50 civilian casualties. Arkan's unit blockaded the barracks and prevented the units of the military police from coming out into the area. Their members killed a JNA captain who was allowed to leave the barracks in order to see his family. He was an ethnic Croat. He was killed in front of the barracks. So he acted very harshly and a large number of persons were killed by his members.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what was the ethnicity of the 50 civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that now, but it is with a great deal of certainty that one could assume that these were Croats rather than Serbs because formally it was at the invitation of Serbs from Bijeljina that he came to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And after the Bijeljina operation in which Arkan and his men engaged in, do you recall whether any political figures came to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that the corps commander came to Bijeljina. He came from Tuzla. And that unit in Bijeljina is from that zone. Biljana Plavsic was there, Fikret Abdic was there, and possibly another person, but it is these three persons that were the key persons there. They were stopped at the entrance into Bijeljina and searched. As a matter of fact, one of these ministers from the Serb government was forced to lie on the ground because he had opposed orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection with regard to the person you cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at 65 ter 1023, this is tab 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- I'm attempting to refresh his recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is an article from "Duga" entitled "Situation in Bijeljina" from around the 12th to the 25th of April, 1992. Can you identify who's depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is Mr. Goran Hadzic, Biljana Plavsic in this photograph, between them is Arkan and I cannot recognise the fourth individual there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Does this refresh your recollection as to who was in Bijeljina from the political side after the operation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, it's leading. It is article from 20 April and the events was on 1st of April. I don't believe that it is connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think the witness can answer the question whether his recollection is refreshed or not. If he does not remember, he just says so. General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember in terms of the information provided by the security organs in Bijeljina that on that day and during that visit of that delegation that came to the barracks that Mr. Hadzic was there. He was not mentioned in that information at all and I don't have any knowledge about him being in Bijeljina on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, the Defence counsel asked you a number of questions about the order issued by Colonel Biorcevic in December 1991 which appeared to place Arkan's unit within the 12th Corps command. Could you tell us, was Colonel Biorcevic ever reprimanded for his attempts to legitimatise Arkan's unit and his activities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. It was the commander of the 1st Military District who was in charge, and we sent the information we had to the SSNO; however, there wasn't any particular reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen P1720. This is tab 96.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during cross-examination on Tuesday, this is at transcript page 8018, you were shown this exhibit, and this is the 1st Military District command order dated 18 November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of the original, page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Defence counsel drew your attention to item 8 of this order -- this is not -- this is not the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While my colleague looks that up, I want to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could go to private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see under number 14 Ljuban Devetak is listed and he's listed as village commander. Based on the information that you had, did the JNA put him in that position of village commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 2 -- oh, before we do, I just want to note for you on items 17 and 18 we have a JNA lieutenant and a JNA captain present at this meeting. But if we could turn to page 2, we see from the heading and the list of persons present at this meeting that this is a meeting of commanders of the Territorial Defence and representatives of the villages of Lovas, Opatovac, Sotin, Tovarnik, and Mohovo, with the deputy minister of the Serbian district and members of the Main Staff of the Serbian district. And if we could turn to page 3 we see that the item on the agenda is the current problems of the Territorial Defence staffs in the liberated places, and under item 1 we se that the meeting was opened by Ljuban Devetak who proposed that the meeting be presided over by this Slobodan Grahovac. First let me ask you, if the JNA was in command of these various TO staffs, who would normally preside over a meeting of those staffs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this information from earlier on, so I can only give my interpretation now. If the Territorial Defence is under the command of the JNA, then these two military persons who were attending would be chairing that meeting. Here it seems that they had been invited by this staff of the Territorial Defence, if that's what it is, that they were invited to this meeting. Probably it had to do with some co-ordination of activity or some other problem in which the army could take part too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like if the witness could read whole text to avoid speculation about the content of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I will, Your Honours, go over some of the provisions or some of the minutes in this meeting. Given the time, I would prefer not to have the witness take the time to read the entire document. That's -- I don't think it's relevant for the purposes of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to say that the purpose of meeting is misstated because the purpose of meeting was another and topic was another, and it is sending of members of TO from these villages to Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Defence counsel's objection is. I read from the document the agenda, item 1. Did -- is that -- need re-translating or did I read that accurately? I'm not sure what the issue is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, what's, in your opinion, the misreading? Mr. Olmsted's misreading?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the purpose of meeting is misstated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: By who? By Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because the purpose of meeting is different, as far as I know this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And where did Mr. Olmsted exactly stated the purpose of the meeting? Could you refer me to the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the page 42. Just a moment. Sorry, I cannot find it. I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. And just for the record, I was simply reading what the document states and under agenda it gives one agenda item and that's what I read, which was: "Current problems of the Territorial Defence staffs in the Liberated Places." I did not summarise this document in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But anyway, let's move on. If we could turn to page 4 of these minutes. If we can look at -- I think it's about two-thirds down the page we see that Jovan Medic from Tovarnik states: "Co-operation with the JNA is good." And if we look a little bit further down we see that Milan Radojcic from Lovas likewise states that: "Co-operation with the JNA is good." If we turn to page 7 at the top we see the JNA Captain Sabo states: "There has to be co-operation ..." And if we look at Lieutenant Marin, he states: "The most significant segment of co-operation with the JNA is in the security goals ..." General, now, in each of these instances the term - and if I mispronounce it - "saradnja" is used for co-operation. How this term used in a military sense, "saradnja"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are activities of two sides that have an approximately equal status. So this is not a relationship between a subordinate and a superior. So that is co-operation in something that is in the common interest, two structures that co-ordinate their activities. It is hard for me to read this handwriting, but I did see from some of the points made in this discussion that there is a reference to the number of volunteers that responded to JNA call-up, 90, 100, perhaps that is a reflection of that co-operation, that they call upon the population in these local communes, that they respond to JNA call-up. That is why they are praising this co-operation. As far as I can interpret it, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 9. We see -- I'm not sure we're on the correct page here or -- yes, we are on the correct page. At the bottom we see that Djuro Prodanovic from Lovas makes a number of conclusions, and just very quickly, 1 is to: "Establish units and TO staffs in the liberated places of this area in accordance with the instructions and tables" with "the competent organs of the Government worked out and sent out." And the second conclusion: "Based on the organisation worked out per the tables from the previous item, it is necessary to step-up co-operation and co-ordination with the JNA billeted in these places." And the third conclusion: "The existing and obvious problems have to be continuously resolved in co-operation with the Government and the relevant military command, such as mopping up the villages, et cetera." General, what do these conclusions indicate to you, regarding the relationship between the JNA and the village TOs in this area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I see that there is a reference to the participation of the government in these activities because they received some schematics. To use military jargon, they got organisational according to which territorial units were supposed to be set up. And secondly, there should be participation, co-operation, assistance from the JNA in that. However, this is a structure that is still not subordinated to the JNA, that is what it looks like from here. These Territorial Defence units are yet to be established. I know from the Lovas case that some parties sent their volunteers and they were practically under the local government of Ljuban Devetak.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2979, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: General, just two more brief issues and then we are done. On Tuesday at transcript page 8023, Defence counsel questioned you about Article 91 of the SFRY Law on All People's Defence, which states: "Any citizen who with weapons or in any other fashion participates in resistance against the enemy is also considered a member of the armed forces." And when you -- these questions were posed to you, at one point you responded: "This law pertains to a much earlier period which only envisioned a situation where the enemy would actually be on the territory of Yugoslavia." First of all, what kind of enemy were you referring to? Was it a domestic enemy? A foreign enemy? Or what -- any kind of enemy?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. An enemy is an aggressor who would be in the territory of Yugoslavia. Secondly, in relation to that question, who could be considered to be a member of the armed forces, I also spoke about those orders that were issued from the SSNO about the admission of volunteers into the JNA. And this probably pertained to members of the Territorial Defence too.
