The requirements to be met by these persons were specified there and that would not only be to have weapons and to be willing to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was it ever envisioned that the -- an armed citizenry would actually become part of the armed forces on its own accord?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this law and the time when it was created, there was a system of All People's Defence in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in which all citizens were involved, in different ways, in resisting the aggressor; that is to say, no armed person could have remained outside the system, either of social self-protection, those units, or Territorial Defence units or the JNA. So this had to do with the inclusion of these persons in organised structures. I would just like to indicate how numerous these units were outside the Territorial Defence and the JNA. Within social self-protection in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were 115.000 persons who were deployed in units of social self protection. And every local common had a unit of its own. So these were not individuals who were armed and who took part in that fighting. They had to be part of a unit, and thereby they became members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this provision aimed at an internal enemy or an external enemy?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm certainly not suggesting an answer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do agree. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The law did not regulate that and did not envision the kind of situation that occurred in 1990 and later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you said that the law did not regulate "that," what did you mean by it did not regulate "that"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the answer of witness is not translated. I could not see it right now. He didn't say that he -- it is not regulated, but that it was not foreseen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Either way, what was not foreseen or what was not regulated?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say what was provided for by the law? If there was internal strife in the country, internal unrest, the immediate jurisdiction over such problems was with the public security, that is, the Ministry of the Interior. It was possible to proclaim the state of emergency in a territory, which did indeed happen in Kosovo in 1981 and 1989, and the first units to be sent there were the units of the MUP because they had jurisdiction over internal conflicts. When those problems grew to proportions that only the army could handle them, then units of the armed forces assisted the MUP. However, a conflict such as this, that one republic becomes a renegade and breaks loose from the whole system, that wasn't provided for by the law. That's why there was self-organisation and areas that didn't want to leave Yugoslavia proclaimed their own autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Finally, yesterday at transcript page 8121 you testified that you learned from the documentation that persons from Vukovar had been beaten before they are brought to the collection centres by the police. First of all, where did those beatings take place by the police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably don't mean which part of the body, but which place geographically. I got information that when the Stajicevo collection centre was opened - and it was done very fast because the citizens of Vukovar were already transferred out of town - the reception of these persons and the first security provided at Stajicevo was provided by MUP organs from Zrenjanin. Only then did JNA officers arrive with the commander of the collection centre with officers from the operative team of the security organs, and after that the ordeal you had to go through when entering the collection centre came to an end because the army had taken over. Then there was a place where MUP organs took persons and that was at Sremska Mitrovica. A note was made of them being mistreated, that they had visible injuries, and there was a reaction to that that was sent to the organs of the interior from where they had come from. These are the essences of the use of force that I remember, force against the persons taken to collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you tell us, were these police officers involving -- involved in the beatings, were they from the Serbian MUP or were they from some other MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were from the Serbian MUP and me thinks that we're talking about personnel securing the KP Dom at Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. General, this is the end of your testimony. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal and for your patience in doing so. You are now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey home. The court usher will escort you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I will take leave, if I may, at this point to turn over the intern to Muireann Dennehy who will lead the next witness. And let me thank the Trial Chamber again for allowing us to sit an extra session today to complete this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the next witness -- for the usher, sorry, to be back and bring in the next witness. Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your question. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mladen Loncar, born on the 4th of May, 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Loncar, you are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witness commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Can I now ask you to may recollect the solemn declaration the court usher gave to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Ms. Dennehy, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and thank you, Your Honours. Before I begin my examination-in-chief, there is a minor procedural point that I would like to raise at this time. It pertains to 65 or proposed 65 ter 6490 and the addition of that document to the Prosecution's exhibit list. This is a document that was disclosed to the Defence on Monday evening and it is a drawing of the Begejci Camp in which the witness was detained, and we would like to add that document to our 65 ter list if possible. We've asked for the Defence's position on that but haven't yet received a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Drawn by whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: By the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a position from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Request granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Currently I work as a psychiatrist at the psychiatric clinic of the clinical hospital centre in Zagreb. I am a specialist in social psychiatry and within that I focus on a discipline called psychotraumatology. Apart from that, I head the national programme for psychosocial help to the victims of the homeland war. I'm the author of the first programme for victims which has two levels. One is our interdisciplinary county centres for social help. There are medical doctors and social workers there. And then the second level is -- can be found at hospitals where psychiatrists who specialise in trauma work. I have worked on this for a number of years and I published some articles especially about the consequences of trauma and traumatic experience --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: -- mostly post-traumatic stress disorder --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Dr. Loncar. If I may, you've just provided the Court with quite a wide range of details about your current profession, if I could just break it down. Since when have you worked in the field of psychotraumatology?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I really began in late 1991 when I was exchanged or in early 1992. I was being trained for a psychiatrist then and then I continued and it's been ongoing until this day. Before the war I worked mostly in the field of neurobiological psychiatry. I began in 1992 at the faculty of medicine, at the department for medical research --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: -- it was with the Ministry of Health --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I apologise. I do apologise for interrupting you. But I would ask you, given the time restraints that we have today, that you please focus specifically on the question that I'm asking you. Can you please tell the Court how many times have you testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: This is my third time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in what cases have you previously testified?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I testified in the Babic case, then the Martic case, and this is the third case.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And in what capacity have you previously testified before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what was the subject matter of that expert testimony?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: That is my area of expertise, namely, the consequences that came about in victims, the consequences of post-traumatic experience. From PTSD to traumatic experience, not only mental and physical but also sexual. I'm referring to women who were victims of rape as well as men who survived a sexual maltreatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now turning briefly to your personal background, can you please tell the Court where you grew up.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, I was born at Donji Gradac in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but when I was 6 months old my parents moved to Ilok and Slavonia. I don't remember the place where I was born because I was a baby. I grew up and went to school at Ilok. This is where I lived and grew.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where did you receive your medical training?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The nearest university for us from Ilok was Novi Sad and that's where I studied medicine. It's about 40 kilometres from Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did -- and when did you graduate from medical school?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I graduated in Novi Sad in 1987/1988.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And following your graduation from medical school in 1987/1988, when did you begin your specialisation in psychiatry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: For a short while I lived in Ilok after graduation. I wanted to work as an intern at Vukovar Hospital but there were no vacancies. That's why I returned to Novi Sad and did my internship there, and I started working on my masters thesis at the psychiatric clinic. And after some time I was employed there, standing in for somebody temporarily. And then I got a permanent position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, the interpreters didn't quite understand your last sentence. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: My specialisation began as a specialisation in neurology and psychiatry. It was -- before the war they were taken as one, but I chose the psychiatric branch.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And you just mentioned the war. How did the outbreak of hostilities in the former Yugoslavia affect your studies?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, I can say what I saw and went through personally. In that area until 1988 when Slobodan Milosevic rose to power, we lived normally and didn't mind who was who. In other words, ethnicity or religion didn't matter to us. Only at about -- or in about 1988 the inter-ethnic tensions started making themselves felt. Then it got worse and the culmination was in 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncar. And how specifically did the rise in ethnic tensions affect your studies in Novi Sad at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I worked normally until 1988. My colleagues were normal, educated people and I had no problems of that kind. But when Slobodan Milosevic rose to power and relations in Yugoslavia deteriorated, what's more, Milosevic introduced an embargo on Slovenian goods. And since Ilok was on the border, my colleagues would give me money so I could buy some Slovenian goods there for them. But with time tensions rose, ethnicity began to matter, and we continued to live multi-culturally but you could feel tension.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And, Dr. Loncar, you just testified in relation to the activities of Milosevic. Were you politically active at the time before or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Before the war I ventured into politics for a short spell when the free and open elections took place in 1990. The democratic alliance of Croats in Vojvodina was founded. I remember that we invited all the parties that were present in Novi Sad, including the ruling party, the Socialist Party of Serbia. It went on for a short while, a couple of months, but then fear started spreading and the initiative faded away spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, you've just told us that the democratic alliance of Croats in Vojvodina was founded. What was the aim of that branch of the Democratic Alliance of Croats?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The ethnic Hungarians had already founded a party of their own. It was a party of ethnic minorities and it advocated the preservation of cultural traditions in that area. We thought that we could contribute to that cultural diversity. In Vojvodina members of over 20 ethnicities lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to the summer of 1991. Where did you spend your annual leave at the end of that summer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: At the time I was specialising in Novi Sad, specialising in psychiatry. I was a novice and, therefore, all the colleagues had priority when it comes to annual leave. And I would also like to add that we had an additional 15 days as psychiatrists. So my annual leave started in early September. I went to my parents' home at Ilok and spent my leave there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And how had the conflict affected the medical services available in Ilok at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Ilok, even before the war, didn't have much in terms of medical infrastructure. There was only an infirmary that was organisationally under Vukovar. There were only a couple of general practitioners active at Ilok and two dentists I think. In late August and early September -- but let me also add that these medical professionals were both Croats and Serbs. But eventually the Serb colleagues stopped coming to work. Most of them lived at Backa Palanka. Two permanently employed doctors, Dr. Grgic and Dr. Holoker remained, they were Croats. They were general practitioners. And during my annual leave I helped them unofficially. We improvised because we had at least two childbirths and I as a psychiatrist didn't have previous experience --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, I again have to interrupt you. I do apologise. I think I'd like again ask you to focus specifically on the questions that I'm putting to you. Maybe I'll rephrase. Can you please tell the Court how the medical supplies available to Ilok were affected by the war?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. At one point in time Ilok was cut off from the rest of Croatia and there was a shortage of medicine of all kinds, which did affect the local population, especially chronic patients and children. There was a shortage of antibiotics and other medicine, shortage of medicine for heart patients, for epilepsy, for treating epilepsy and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what did you do in order to help the chronic patients and children in Ilok at the end of summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, I talked to my colleagues because I was rather mobile, I had a car too, and I was not afraid, and I didn't think that there was anything bad going on. I went to buy medicine for certain patients in Ilok. I remember, among others, medicine that was needed for a child that was treated for epilepsy, and the parents asked me in particular to look for that in Novi Sad. So I went to Novi Sad to buy a certain amount of medicine for the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And when did you travel to Novi Sad to buy that medicine?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection it was on the 1st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time. I think now might be an appropriate time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Dennehy. Mr. Loncar, we take a break now, a break of 30 minutes, and come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy, just for planning purposes, now you've felt the witness, what is your estimation about the timing of your chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do think I'll take most of the three hours that I have been allocated in relation to this witness. I will attempt and try and control the witness to the extent I can and focus him; however, I do think, given the number of documents and the information that I need to get from this witness, I will take close to three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the Defence, any idea? Will it be three hours or will it be less? I mean three hours is what you theoretically are entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Far less than three hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But then reasonably, we will not finish the witness today; right? We have one hour and a half when we come back -- one hour and a quarter, and we have one hour and a half tomorrow -- sorry, this afternoon. Right? So that -- you will take all that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I don't expect to take all of that time. I will use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's two hours, 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: That's correct. I will do my best to limit my examination-in-chief to the extent I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But obviously or at least reasonably that means that we will, if we want to finish this witness this week and not let him stay over the weekend and with regard to the next week's planning, we should sit tomorrow morning as well for one session?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, I think it would be best to allocate time in the morning; however, I would hope that we wouldn't have to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we know where we are, and by all means you are entitled to a maximum of the hearing this afternoon and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I suppose you would all think that I would come back to the planning, but I must say I'm speechless. So let's just continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Loncar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Dennehy.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, before we resume, can I please ask whether you feel okay following the alarm earlier and that you are okay to continue?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, before the break you told us that on the 1st of October, 1991, you travelled to Novi Sad in order to obtain medical supplies for the people of Ilok. Can you please tell the Court what happened to you as you drove from Novi Sad back to Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I just may, a sentence or two why I left Ilok. Already on the 1st of October, when I went to Novi Sad, before that in Ilok there was a humanitarian crisis. In Ilok there were a lot of people who actually came from the neighbouring villages. There were major shortages of everything, food, medicine, and the local population and refugees came to seek help. Also, there was a great deal of fighting around Vukovar, even in Ilok, that's 35 kilometres away from Vukovar. One could feel the vibrations of these cannons or whatever they were. A day before I left, I had the opportunity of helping at the infirmary when a refugee came from Tovarnik who had a gun-shot wound in his arm and he told us about all sorts of terrible things that were happening. Dr. Grgic and Dr. Holoker asked me after that, since I worked in Novi Sad, asked me if I could go and buy some medicine and help prevent a very bad thing from happening in Ilok. So there weren't any checks on the bridge. The army, the JNA, held the bridge --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: -- towards Backa Palanka --

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: -- I'm afraid that we have very, very limited time today and therefore I must ask you again to focus specifically on the questions that I'm putting to you. This information is, of course, helpful, but it is more helpful to answer the questions that I am putting. So if I can ask my question again: What happened to you as you left Novi Sad and drove back to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: At that moment I was driving a friend of mine, Ivan Suvak, and I stopped in front of his house, a parking-lot there, and some policemen jumped out of this Kombi van, some were in uniform, some were in plain clothes. They asked me for the key and they put me into this police car and they took me to the provincial SUP, the SUP of the province. They were saying along the way, "Here he is." They took this appeal that I wrote in Novi Sad, because before that I saw a friend, a priest in Petrova Radan, Marko Kljajic, who gave me money for medicine and that's where I wrote this appeal asking for international observers and possibly Doctors Without Borders to come help us, that the proportions of the humanitarian crisis were growing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, you said some policemen jumped out of a car. How many policemen were there that arrested you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, as far as I could see then - I was taken by surprise - I think there were six or seven of them, some of them in uniform and other in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And you said that they brought you to the office of the provincial SUP. Where was that office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It's in Novi Sad. That was the centre of the then-milicija, police. It was a building.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Court what happened to you at the SUP building in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, they brought me into some space. They came in by car and then they took me to the third floor. They took me to a room and then a uniformed policeman walked in. He talked to me for about five minutes. He took my details. And then policemen started coming in, policemen in civilian clothing. And they started putting questions, tortures started, beatings, et cetera. They kept me that way for about 30 hours, without a break, without giving me any time to sleep. I could just go to the toilet once. They were putting two sets of questions to me. One set had to do with Ilok and the other had to do with this brief activity of mine within the Democratic Alliance of Croats in Vojvodina. They beat me mercilessly. I was wearing a jeans jacket and I just had a T-shirt underneath, a white T-shirt, and they pulled that up and -- in fact, they tied my hands with my jacket and they beat me on the head and torso with a bat that was about 90 centimetres long. It wasn't a classical baton. They were hitting me on the back, on the head, and they kept asking me who my connection was, who I was in contact with. They started asking me about some alleged connections of mine, and I never knew this man, Laszlo Tot who was the editor of the Hungarian programme on Novi Sad TV. They asked who I socialised with from the Hungarian community in Novi Sad, then also in Ilok, what units were there, what was there. That would be it, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncar. You've just provided us with quite a bit of information. I'd like to go back over that so we can clarify some of this. You said: "They beat me mercilessly. "... they beat me with a bat that was about 90 centimetres long." When you say "they," who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What I came to realise then was that they were policemen in plain clothes, but I don't think it was the crime prevention police, I think it was the secret police judging by the questions that they put. I came to believe, especially later on, that this was no crime prevention police but rather the secret police that was questioning me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncar. And how many policemen or members of the secret police questioned you there in the SUP headquarter building in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: There were two that were there all the time, but then five or six kept changing during those 30 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And you told us earlier that they beat you with a bat that was approximately 90 centimetres long. It wasn't a classical baton. Can you please describe what weapon they used to beat you with.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I don't know. There was leather on the outside. It wasn't that classical police baton, truncheon, that you'd see in the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You said that they beat you on the head and torso. What injuries did you sustain as a result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have to say that they didn't only use the batons. One of the two policemen who were there all the time, let's say that they were the chief interrogators, one of them -- well, he was the one who hit me in the nose here, on the face. Thankfully he was wearing tennis shoes only, so my nose started to bleed and they even gave me a cloth at one moment so that I'd stop the blood because it started flowing down my body and I had hematoma on my back, on my chest.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You told us earlier that you were interrogated for approximately 30 hours. What did you do after you were released from your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: After that interrogation they released me. I was dizzy. Although I knew Novi Sad well at the time, I couldn't orientate myself, so they showed me the way. I came to my rented room and I asked the landlady for painkillers and on the following day I went to a clinic. I complained to my bosses and my colleagues at the clinic, telling them what had happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You've just told us the following day you went to a clinic. Is that your place of work that you returned to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, my place of work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were you ever arrested again by the secret police in Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime -- I mean, from this first arrest which I will never forget with that beating, it went on for some 30 hours. In the period after that, four or five or six times I was taken away from work. My vacation was over and I started working and usually they would come in the afternoon, they would come to my work, and they'd pick me up and they'd take me to the same place, at the provincial SUP. Every time I was brought in there were interrogations followed with beatings. They slapped my face. Every time I had to write statements as I was handcuffed to a table. Then they'd give me a piece of paper and I'd have to write with my other hand. Among other things, they were forcing me to write that I was the founder of the war hospital in Ilok, which I had to do under duress. And when that was over, I'd have to write the same content and then I'd have to write that Dr. Tomo Grgic wrote -- established this hospital, although there was no such hospital, there was no possibility, there were no conditions for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you've just told us you were taken some four or five or six times from the hospital where you worked. How often were you taken to be interrogated at the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, approximately every two or three days they would take me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you please tell us when the last time -- your last interrogation took place at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, it was around the 4th or the 5th or the 6th of November, 1991. I don't know the exact date, as I don't remember it any longer, the last time when I was called for questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And after this interrogation took place on the 5th of November, 1991, where were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The two who were there and who I believed were the main interrogators handcuffed me, they put my hands behind my back. In the evening they put me into the official car and they started across the Danube from Novi Sad. So we left the city. We came to the Srem side of the Danube, and they continued towards Beocin and Ilok. At one moment before Beocin, because I could see the sign, they turned into Fruska Gora; that is to say, into the mountain, into the woods. I didn't know where or why they were taking me, and I think that they even lost their way at one moment so that they turned back on the road. And I was thinking about the worst at the time. I believed that we were going somewhere where I would meet my end, but they continued to drive along the country road and we came at one point in front of a building where there were soldiers. So judging by that, I realised that they had brought me to some kind of barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what armed forces were in charge of the barracks, to the place where you were brought?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: What I saw was that this was the military police. There were three majors present as well as one lieutenant. Judging by what followed, I came to realise that these were, as I had served the former JNA and I know a few things, these were the security organs, the military security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you now know the name of the place to -- the place that you were brought?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: This place is called Paragovo. It's in Fruska Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where were you detained in Paragovo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: They took me into the main building and then there was a staircase down which the guards took me into the basement which was -- it had an oval shape and there were steel bars and there were already some people inside, people wearing civilian clothes who were detained. There were the planks as well and they threw me in and I stayed there until the morning, or rather, I stayed there for the next three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, you've just said there were people already there wearing civilian clothing who were being -- who were detained. How many people were already in detention when you arrived at Paragovo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: According to my estimate, there were more than ten people. I know that it was quite crowded and we had to lay there all squeezed together on these planks.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How did the guards treat you and the other prisoners while you were detained at Paragovo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: All three days, on a daily basis, approximately every hour they would come and force us to get up. We would have to thrust our hands and arms through the bars and they would beat us on our hands, and then during the night every hour or two they would wake us up and force us to get up. They wouldn't let us sleep. Possibly they would take someone out from the bars because there was a small space that was meant for them as the guards, and then they would beat this person there in that enclosure.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while you were detained at Paragovo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. Two majors interrogated me. I am aware of their ranks because they were uniformed and, as I said I know these ranks from the time when I had served the JNA. So I know that they were majors by ranks. Again, there were two sets of questions, one of which referred to Ilok and the other one about my supposed acquaintances and connections in Novi Sad; inter alia, I was interrogated also by a lieutenant. As he was the only one who did not beat me, I asked him at one point, "Why don't you take me to court if I'm guilty of anything?" And he said, "We have no elements to bring charges against you, but you can choose to which camp you would be sent, whether you want to be sent to a camp in Serbia or in the SAO Krajina." To which I said, "I live and work in Novi Sad, so if it comes to this then let me be sent somewhere in Serbia." On the third day of my stay in Paragovo, a third major arrived. He said that he had searched my family house. He shouted, he insulted, he was very rude, but he didn't give me any information nor was he able to find anything that would compromise me in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you've just told us that there were three majors present at Paragovo who all interrogated you. To what unit or specific unit did those majors belong, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Judging by what they asked me and how, I concluded that they belonged to the JNA service which is called the counter-intelligence service or the abbreviation is K-O-S, KOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And, Dr. Loncar, you've just told us that you were interrogated also by a lieutenant and he was the only one who did not beat you. Are you therefore saying that you were beaten by the other -- by the majors at Paragovo?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, they slapped me.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, you've said as well earlier that you spent three days at Paragovo. Where were you transferred to from Paragovo when you left there?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: One day, that was the third day I think, it was in the afternoon, that together with one or two other men they put me in a military police vehicle which had the insignia VP, standing for Vojna Policija, military police. We were able to sit inside, but we could not see anything on the outside. There was a dim light inside the vehicle and they drove us between one and two hours according to my estimate. Occasionally a soldier would just open the small window that was there and look at us through the glass to check us out and that was all. After between one and two hours, I could feel that we were now on an unpaved road, judging by the movements of the vehicle. So after the said time had elapsed, we had reached our destination and the car stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You said: "We reached our destination and the car stopped." Where had you reached at that point?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I didn't know at the moment where we were, but when the vehicle stopped I could hear people speaking outside and there was someone who asked, "Are they tied?" At that moment the doors of the van were opened. We got out and at that moment I witnessed a scene which was astonishing. It was like something I had seen in the movies or had read about. Flash-lights were on because it was night-time. There were dogs barking but they were behind some wiring so they couldn't get out. There was a stable in front of us and on the side were standing people, that is to say soldiers. And we got out and were between the soldiers who were lined in two ranks. And at that moment they tried beating us savagely, so we then realised that we had to get up at any cost, as much as our strength would hold out, because if we fell to the ground we could be kicked in to the head which could be fatal. So that even though I stumbled due to the blows, I would manage to get up every time. And by passing through this gauntlet that we had to run, there were five or six soldiers on each side. We eventually entered the stable through the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And what is the name of the stable that you reached and you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: These were Begejci. That was the camp in Begejci.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You've just said that you were forced to run a gauntlet with soldiers on either side. How many soldiers were in that gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: According to my estimate, as far as something like that is possible to estimate at such a moment, there were in total about ten or so of them. It's difficult to say exactly. There could have been one or two less.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You said that: "They tried beating us savagely." What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: They beat us with their hands, with their feet, and with truncheons or whatever they could get hold of. Fortunately they did not have long-barrelled arms but just pistols. They did not take them out. They only beat us with truncheons and with the boots that were on their feet and also with their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How did you feel after arriving at Begejci and being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, it was a sort of astonishment. It was something I had never had a chance to see in real life up until that point. It's something that I still remember as some kind of film. It seemed unreal at the moment, that there was such a stable in which they eventually took us that was fenced off with double wiring 2 metres high with the guard posts with flash-lights and with German shepherd dogs who made a horrible noise while barking because they were excited and they were behind the wire. And what I thought for myself was: My God, they have brought me to a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, I'd like to now show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that tab 18 of the Court's bundle be shown to the witness, that is 65 ter 6490, and it's page 1 that I would like the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the diagram which I drew to the best of my recollection and which depicts the Begejci camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature on that document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, you've described some of the camp just now to the Court. You said that it was fenced off with double wiring, there were dogs. Can you please describe to the Court the layout of the camp by reference to the document in front of you, so using the letters A, B, C, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I will use those letters. Under A is the building of the command. I realised that during my detention, that that was the command of the camp. Under B was the main entrance to the camp because the entire camp was surrounded by barbed wire and there were guards all around but there were special guards at the entrance. Under C is a small building. I never had a chance to see what that really was. D is the fence around the camp, the outside camp. F is the entrance to the stable where the inmates were accommodated. E stands for the double line of barbed wire where the main facility, that is to say the stable, was because it was fenced off. Under E are the spotlight --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- under G are the spotlight reflectors that I saw as soon as I got there because they were used to light the whole complex for the camp. Under H are the guards' houses, something like machine-gun nests. I on the side stands for "improvised toilets" because there were holes that were dug out in the ground and fenced off with nylon. Under J that was a bucket with water where from a glass all the inmates would be served water. Under L within the camp complex were the eves.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncar, again having the document in front of you that you've just described, what did the guards at the camp tell you about the fence that you have marked as D?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, they threatened us. They said that we should never think of trying to flee because there was an electrical current running along the fence, so we never dared even to come close to this fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where were the prisoners held, again, referring to the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The inmates were under the building depicted with the letter K. That was the building, the stable which dated from the times of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. I think it was an abandoned farm and it was around 50 metres long and around 10 metres wide with a door that was never closed. There was a concrete floor and on the sides I know that it used to be a stable because there were these places that used to contain food for the cattle.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that there were German shepherd dogs who made a horrible noise. Where did the dogs patrol, by reference to the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: They patrolled in this section between the two rows of wiring. That was where the dogs were held. The double wiring was only around the main camp building, that is to say the stable in which we were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And you told us that H noted the machine-gun nests. How high were those towers or the machine-gun nests?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Around 3 metres high, 2 and a half to 3 metres as far as I could assess.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How many prisoners were detained at the stamp at the letter K, so within the main stable?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Between 500 and 600 at the end. I know that it was approximately that number because in the evening they used to call out our names and then we had to respond by saying what our numbers were, first, second, third, et cetera. And I know that they counted 500 something. And then my answer would be between 500 and 600 prisoners in the stables there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And were there any female prisoners in the stable?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, there were. My estimate is between 25 and 30 women.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you know who the camp commander was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The letter A here, this area where the command of the prison was, in that facility there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you know the name of the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, he introduced himself, Lieutenant-Colonel Miroslav Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, earlier you described a gauntlet that consisted of approximately ten soldiers. How many guards or soldiers were present in total at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, since our movement was restricted and we had to keep our hands at our backs and our heads down, if I were to give an estimate I would say that approximately within that compound there were between 30 to 50 guards and officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And to what unit did these guards or officers belong?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: During detention they would take us to -- out for interrogation, so I came to the conclusion that they were members of the counter-intelligence service, they were security organs judging by the questions that were put to us. As for the guards, some of them had insignia, others were without insignia. They were members of the military police of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now can we scroll to page 2 of the document, of 65 ter 6490, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you'll shortly see another document in front of you. Can you tell the Court what is depicted in this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I drew a sketch here of the compound of the camp itself where the inmates were. So this is double wire, then also the spotlights, the guards' hut, and then the stable here, that was the central facility where we were with this door that was never closed, then here, I'm showing it to you right now, there was a small table with a chair where the officer would write down our names when the guards would bring us in. Then they would force us to line up. When I was brought to Begejci camp, I was here roughly. I came to here. All of this was full here, so almost half of the camp was full at the time when I arrived. So these little lines show how we were lined up in the camp, how we were lying there. So basically we were like sardines in a tin, just a bit of straw on concrete.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I please ask that the 65 ter 6490 be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2918, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you've just told the Court that you were lying like sardines in the stable. How were the prisoners forced to position themselves in the stable, can you describe how you were forced to lie?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: When the camp was full, that is to say when I arrived the camp was full and they -- the guards said that they were waiting for the rest, for the Ustashas after the fall of Vukovar. That's what they said. Indeed, people from Vukovar were being brought in and then this line was full and then this other line opposite the other wall. So then there was very little space left. If one could sleep at night at all, one would have to lie on the side. When the guards would walk in, then we would all have to lie on our stomachs with our heads down so that we would not see who they were calling out and taking out.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncar, I'd like to show you another document, and you'll see shortly on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: May I ask that tab 12, that is 65 ter 6462, be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. When arriving in camp, we would have all our belongings taken away from us, whatever we had on us at that point in time. And then they would list all the things that they found on me. So there was some money, my ID, my driver's licence, traffic licence, car registration, watch, coupons showing the value of the individual coupons, and this down here is the signature of the officer who took all of this. I was no exception there. Everyone who entered the stable or the camp had all their belongings taken away from them. Among others, there were quite a few elderly persons there with chronic illnesses from neighbouring villages, between Ilok and Vukovar, that is, who came with small bags of medicine, and so on. All of that was taken away from them and we could do nothing in camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, just to clarify, the items that you just named, specifically money, my ID, driver's licence, those are noted on the document in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I please ask that the 65 ter 6462 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, I'd now like to turn to the conditions at the camp. You've described part of those conditions, but I'd like to develop that further. When you arrived in Begejci in November of 1991, how cold was it outside?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, I mean, it is well-known that in Vojvodina at that time of year it is rather cold and a wind called Kosava usually blows at the time. The temperature was below 0, I believe. It would even be minus 10 outside. That was just an estimate. We had no way of checking. It was terribly cold, especially because this door was never closed. The only way we could get warmer was because there were so many of us there, 500, 600. We were so crowded in there, one next to the other, lying next to each other. During the day we were not allowed to move about. We had to sit there except for when they'd allow us for about half an hour to walk within the confines of that barbed wire and that was it. So in addition to those conditions, that temperature, until the Red Cross arrived we just had straw when the Red Cross came. Then before the other time when they came they would give us a blanket each, although that was not sufficient because there was concrete down there. There were concrete floors and sub-0 temperatures outdoors and the door was always open. On the other hand, hygienic conditions were terrible. We had to ask for permission to go to these improvised toilets behind the stable. We would be beaten every time we went out so that some people would try not to go to the toilet for a few days, since they were afraid that they would be beaten yet again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Loncar. I'm just going to go back over some of what you told us. You said it was approximately minus 10 outside. Was the stable building heated for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: No. The building did not have any kind of heating. What made it even more difficult was the fact that there were some small windows there and then there was no glass on some of them and the wind would blow day and night so it would be even colder in that stable, and those who were next to the door they, in fact, slept as if they were sleeping outdoors as far as the temperature is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that the hygienic conditions were terrible. What sanitary facilities were there at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The sanitary conditions were as follows. The inmates who arrived before I came dug a few pits and then there was plastic between them, and these were our toilets. That's when we went out to the toilet. There was no hand washing, there was no water except for limited quantities of drinking water that we were given. So we were quite unkempt. They took away all our personal belongings, including anything that resembled shavers. That's the way it was until we -- the Red Cross came to see us. Then they found one of the inmates who had allegedly been a barber before the war, and then he used the same shaver to shave all of us and to give us haircuts. Among us there was already lice. Some of us already had lice because of the hygienic conditions that existed there. Other people had intestinal trouble because after leaving the toilet there was no possibility of washing one's hands or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you've just said: "There was no water except for limited quantities of drinking water ..." And earlier on the document that I showed you, you indicated that that water was at position J. Can you describe how much water was available to the 500-odd prisoners at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Well, it was a bucket full of water. It's hard for me to describe it, pretty big. Perhaps its capacity was, say, between 10 or 20 litres of water, and then there was a glass that we all used to drink water.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: How many glasses were there for the 500-odd prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I only know of one, it was by the bucket. We would be given -- or rather, we would be given that glass to have a drink of water when we approached the bucket.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You told us earlier that several of the prisoners developed lice because of the hygienic conditions that existed at the camp. What other diseases was common amongst the prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Apart from lice, people often complained of intestinal problems, especially diarrhea. I suppose that it was caused by poor hygiene.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Were any of the camp detainees ordered to carry out forced labour?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. They singled out a group of inmates who went outside the camp to clear a wood, an overgrown area; that happened daily. We were not allowed to talk among ourselves, but we did hear some information. Before leaving the camp, they first had to cut a stick which the guards then used to drive them during the forced labour. And if I may continue? Furthermore, they were saying that civilians were also being brought, probably from the surrounding villages or passers-by, and they would point out the inmates and say, "These are -- these people are Ustashas." And some of those civilians would beat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the interrogations that took place at the camp, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. During my stay I was interrogated five to six times by some officers, and I must add that civilian police was there at least once from the provincial SUP. I was taken to be interrogated some five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And where were you interrogated? What building?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The interrogations took place at the command building of the camp. There were some rooms in which there was usually an officer with a guard, a soldier, and we had to answer their questions. That was one thing. And additionally we had to write down statements. Those statements were mostly coerced. People would write anything in those statements because they had been tortured and beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, I'm afraid the interpreters have asked if you can repeat the sentences that followed: "People would write anything in those statements ..." The interpreters didn't quite catch what you said.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, those officers ordered them what to write. I had to write, for example, that I had been head of the -- of a war time hospital which never existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Otherwise they wouldn't stop beating the person in question until he wrote something.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You said that there was usually an officer and a soldier present. To what units did those officers belong?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I was able to conclude on the basis of their questions that the interrogators belonged not to the military police but they were KOS officers. They interrogated us, in fact, and ordered us what to write.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You just told us that: "Otherwise they wouldn't stop beating the person in question until he wrote something." Were you beaten during the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. The system of interrogation was the following. In that room we would be beaten. It was mostly the guard who mostly was already inside and when signalled by the officer he would start beating us. If not there, then upon returning to the barn the guards would continue to beat certain persons. They would always target someone. And we found out that either they would be sent to be interrogated tomorrow and therefore beaten today or he was interrogated yesterday and beaten after the interrogation. That was a way of breaking people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: What injuries did you personally sustain as a result of the beatings during the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: I had regular hematomas and for a couple of days I was hardly able to move when the military policeman or guard hit me so forcefully with his elbow in the lower part of the cervical spine that I had terrible pain and for days I had great difficulty moving. My movements were very limited.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You told us that the interrogations did take place in the command building which is separate from the stable. Before being taken for interrogation, can you describe the atmosphere in the stable amongst the prisoners as the guards came to select prisoner for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: The rule was such that we had all to lie flat on our bellies with our hands under our heads or eyes, actually. And since we knew that somebody would be taken away, you couldn't hear a sound. And I had the feeling that I heard my heart beating. And the other, or rather, the only sound that you could hear was soldiers' boots walking on concrete and you could tell if someone was approaching you or walking away, and of course as a result you were more or less scared. Sometimes, or rather, when they kicked you in the -- in the feet, that was a sign that you were supposed to get up. Sometimes they would beat people in the stable but we were not allowed to watch. From there, the people would be taken to the command building.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: You said that sometimes they would beat people in the stable but we were not allowed to watch. How did you know that they were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Because, as I said, it was totally quiet. All 500 of us were so scared that nobody dared move. It was -- there was dead silence and the only thing you could hear were blows. So it was easy to tell that somebody was being beaten, and of course you could hear the whimpering of that person being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, I'd now like to show you another document and you'll see that appear on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Can I ask that tab 4, that's 65 ter 2916.3, be shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, do you recognise the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes. It's a list of the prisoners at the Begejci camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signature on the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature. I'd signed this list when I reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If we could now scroll to page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, there are circles around two of the names on this list. Can you please explain what the circles mean.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: It means that I met those people at the camp. They are people from Ilok and I had known them from before. They were elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: If we can move to page 5 of this document, and I would please ask that it not be broadcast at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, there's a circle around Krunoslav Farkas on this document. What happened to Mr. Farkas?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Let me first say that I knew Mr. Farkas from Ilok. During our detention he was beaten so badly that he lapsed into a post traumatic delirium as we call it. He totally lost orientation toward himself and his surroundings. On one occasion he -- he was tied with wire and said, "I'm going home now." He had no sense of reality. I cannot say exactly how much later, but a couple of years after being exchanged he died. I believe that this was a consequence of the torture he was subjected to at the camp. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, the name Zlatko Brajer is marked on this document in front of you and circled. Is that the correct name, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: Yes, though I must note that as so much time has elapsed, more than 20 years, he's stuck in my memory because I participated in his reanimation. Zlatko is certainly his first name. I'm not sure whether it was Brajer or Brajovic that was his last name, but that was him, from Vukovar. I know that he was a retired teacher because after the exchange his wife reached me in Zagreb and I then wrote a medical certificate confirming that he had been killed in the Begejci camp by being beaten up. Why did I have to do that? Because one day the commander of the camp, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, ordered me to come to the command building, and there outside next to the door Zlatko was lying on the floor. At the moment when I got there, he was not showing any signs of life, and I then attempted to revive him. I lifted up the clothes he had on the upper part of his body. He was all covered in hematoma. And when I tried to massage his heart, I realised at that moment that all his ribs had been broken because there was no resistance by the ribs. My hand would just sink in, and I tried for a while, for about a minute, to do this, but I could just note that he had died.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Dr. Loncar, you'd said that the commander of the camp, Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, ordered you to come to the command building. Was that the first time you had been ordered to go to the command building by the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: There was another occasion on which he ordered me to do so in another case, the case of Zoran Sipos, as far as I remember. He was brought there in the afternoon and I was then called by Lieutenant-Colonel Zivanovic, the commander of the camp, to try and calm him down because he had been beaten up and he was telling that in front of the camp commander, that he had been beaten savagely at the Stajicevo camp and he was then brought there. I was also told to see what he could be given and I told him that he should be given medication that would calm him down and also some painkillers. I don't know what happened later on, but he had visible injuries on his face in the form of hematoma and he was complaining himself. He had been beaten so badly that it seemed to me that it was all the same to him what the commander would hear or not, that he was in such an agitated state and that he just wanted to tell about his experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: I'd like to now return to Zlatko Brajovic who you spoke of. When you tried to resuscitate him, where was the camp commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: At that moment he was entering the room, and when the guard brought me he was already behind me in this room with the open door where Zlatko lay down on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: And can you describe how Zlatko appeared when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: As someone who had lost his consciousness, there was no activity. He wasn't moving at all. So I approached him and what I tried to see or feel was to feel his pulse but I couldn't find it, which meant that his heart had stopped. I then put my ear close to his face to hear whether he was breathing and I couldn't hear that, and therefore I started to resuscitate him. And then I realised that his ribs had been broken because we had learned that in the practice that as students at the faculty of medicine. So I know what it looks like when you try to resuscitate a man when his ribs are complete, and when your hands sinks in because there's no resistance whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Loncar, my final question in relation to the document in front of you is: You marked some of the names on this list with an X. What does that X depict without naming any of the people in question?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN LONCAR
utterances.text: These are the persons who were with us in the camp and who I suspected at the time were victims of sexual abuse. Later on, as I will explain, my then suspicions turned out to be true and that that was precisely the case, rape.

utterances.speaker: MS. DENNEHY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may tender this 65 ter 6490 into evidence under seal -- sorry, I do apologise. I got the number wrong. It's 65 ter 2916.3 into evidence under seal, and there is a publicly redacted version of that document at 65 ter 2916.4, and that is loaded to e-court and released.
